spain-high-speed-train-crash.headline: High-speed train crash in Spain kills at least 68
spain-high-speed-train-crash.body_md:
A Renfe high-speed train ran into the back of a stopped Iryo train on the Madrid–Seville line on Wednesday morning, killing at least 68 people. It is one of the deadliest rail accidents in Europe in years. Officials say the toll may rise. The first official account of the cause is stark, but it is preliminary, and the independent investigation has not yet reported.

## What happened

The collision came at about 8:30am local time at kilometre marker 118, near the town of Urda. That is roughly 150km south of Madrid, in Toledo province and between the towns of Mora and Orgaz. Both trains were heading from Madrid to Seville. According to figures reported by ABC News, the Renfe service carried 397 passengers and the Iryo service, number 6076, carried 146, including a baby.

Authorities said the Renfe train probably struck the Iryo train from behind. Two coaches derailed and fell down an embankment. Castilla-La Mancha's regional president, Emiliano García-Page, said 24 of the dead were on the Renfe train and the rest on the Iryo train. At least 15 people were seriously hurt and more than 50 others were treated for lesser injuries, though counts differ between outlets. The US State Department said several American citizens were injured but that none were among the dead so far. Canadian officials reported six Canadians hurt.

Survivors described confusion and fear. Miguel Ángel Pérez, who was in the last car of the Renfe train, said it had stopped because of what he understood to be an overload on the track, then restarted. He then felt an impact and the train tilting as it derailed. Ana, who was hurt in the face and leg, said passengers broke windows to get out and that firefighters pulled her from the wreckage. She described people dying around her. A Florida tourist said the train was "completely destroyed" and that people were covered in blood.

Emergency services, military rescue units and search dogs worked through the wreckage. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the site, and Spain declared three days of official mourning from Thursday to Saturday. Iryo cancelled all its services out of Madrid-Puerta de Atocha on the southern corridor, with no date for resumption.

## An early explanation, and its limits

Transport Minister Óscar Puente has said the preliminary inquiry points to an "inexplicable" order from rail controllers. By his account, a computer failure first halted six moving trains. The control centre then let them move again without speed restrictions, and the Renfe train ran into the stationary Iryo train ahead of it. Puente called the episode "truly unbelievable."

That is a minister's early reading, not a finding. The independent railway accident investigation commission is responsible for determining the cause, and such bodies usually take months to publish a full report. Several questions are open. They include why the computer failure occurred, why the trains were released, what protections should have stopped a following train from closing on a stationary one, and whether human error or system design was the deeper fault. Even if an individual decision proves central, investigators typically ask why the system allowed one decision to have such consequences.

## A second disaster in ten months

The crash revives memories of an earlier one. In January, Iryo and Renfe trains collided near Adamuz in Córdoba province, killing 46 people. García-Page said the causes of the two accidents appear to be unrelated. If that holds, the cause here lies in control-room procedure rather than the track or the trains, but the public may not draw that distinction.

Wednesday's death toll is the highest for a Spanish high-speed accident since 2013. That year 80 people died when a train derailed at Santiago de Compostela in Galicia. Spain has built one of the world's largest high-speed networks, and since the market was opened to competition, private operators such as Iryo have run services alongside state-owned Renfe. Two serious accidents involving trains of both companies in a single year will raise questions about the oversight of a busier, more crowded corridor. The evidence so far does not assign blame to the competitive model, and the investigation may not either.

The wider stake is confidence in a flagship low-carbon form of travel. Rail is cheap, fast and heavily promoted as an alternative to short-haul flying, and that case depends on a reputation for safety.

## What to watch

The death toll is likely to be revised as the search of the wreckage ends. The next markers are the commission's interim findings and any decision on how quickly the southern corridor reopens. Also due are answers on the control-centre procedures Puente described, which will show whether the failure was one controller's error or a gap in the rules. Those answers will decide whether the response stays in Spain or leads to changes in how other networks manage signalling failures.
spain-high-speed-train-crash.in_one_sentence: A Renfe high-speed train hit a stopped Iryo train near Toledo, killing at least 68; the transport minister blames an 'inexplicable' control order, but investigators have not yet reported.

immigration-agents-data-leak.headline: Hack leaks details of thousands of US immigration agents
immigration-agents-data-leak.body_md:
Records on more than 41,000 staff at the US Department of Homeland Security have been published online, including thousands who work in immigration enforcement. The BBC reported the leak on Wednesday. It turns a data breach into a safety question for officers and their families.

The material includes names, work addresses, phone numbers and descriptions of each person's work. By the BBC's count, more than 21,000 of those listed work for Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and nearly 6,600 for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Other records cover Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The data also names dozens of previously unknown operations, the agents who led or worked on them, and the tools they used, including products from Cellebrite and Palantir.

This account rests on the BBC's reporting as syndicated by Yahoo. The database itself was not examined, and the agency has confirmed only a potential breach.

## Who published it, and why

A group calling itself the Department of Peace says it took the information from DHS. The journalist and security researcher maia crimew and the transparency group Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets) published it in a searchable database called "Icepick". DDoSecrets previously hosted BlueLeaks, the 2020 release of US police data.

The publishers say it is not a full directory of DHS agents. DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability". Best said the data identifies officials overseeing covert operations, the government's hunt for leakers and personnel in deportation programmes.

The Department of Peace's spokesperson pointed to ICE's conduct and to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who took the job in March. The spokesperson cited his July statement that he was "turning up the heat".

The group said it reached the agent profiles through Okta, the single sign-on service that controls staff logins to internal systems. An Okta spokeswoman said the company knows of the claims but that "Okta is secure". She said it has no evidence its data or systems were compromised. How the intruders actually got in is therefore unresolved.

## The safety question

DHS said it is aware of a potential breach and is working to address it. A spokesperson said the department takes threats against employees seriously and will update the public when more information is available. The agency has not said whether it can verify the records.

The exposure matters because of how enforcement work is now done. Agents often work masked and rarely identify themselves, though the law requires it, and politicians have pressed DHS to enforce that rule. ICE agents have shot more than two dozen people this year and killed at least nine, according to the BBC, including Renée Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota, neither of whom was an arrest target. Anonymity is a safety measure for officers. It is also a point of contention for critics who want those officers identifiable and answerable. The leak lands in the middle of that dispute.

It is also not the first. In January, details of about 4,500 ICE and Border Patrol employees reached the activist site ICE List, which said a DHS whistleblower supplied them. The BBC describes this one as the third such government leak or hack in recent weeks. It cites the ShinyHunters group's breach of the FBI last month, which took personal information on thousands of agents, and a suspected hacking attempt that took the Federal Election Commission offline.

## What to watch

Two questions will decide how serious this becomes: whether DHS confirms the records are authentic, and whether it explains the access route, given Okta's denial. The department has promised an update. How far the data spreads beyond the Icepick site, and whether any individuals are targeted as a result, will show whether the safety risks officers fear materialise.

apple-iphone-screen-replacement.headline: Apple to replace iPhones affected by a screen fault
apple-iphone-screen-replacement.body_md:
Apple is running a replacement programme for iPhones with a faulty display, according to a BBC Technology report. Beyond that, little is confirmed. The report as it reached this desk does not say which models are affected, how many handsets are involved, when the programme began, or what is causing the fault. Those gaps limit what can responsibly be said about it.

## What is known

The core fact is that Apple is offering to replace devices with a display problem. That is a company-run remedy, not a customer-initiated warranty claim. The distinction matters, because a programme usually means Apple has decided the fault is common enough, or clearly enough a manufacturing defect, to justify fixing it even for owners whose standard warranty has lapsed.

It is not yet established whether this is a formal recall. Apple has historically avoided that word for display faults. It tends to use "service programme" instead, which lets owners keep using their phones and book a free repair or replacement when convenient. Whether this one follows that pattern is unconfirmed.

Searches on 29 October 2026 turned up no Apple notice or other coverage that matched this programme, so the model range, eligibility window and affected serial numbers remain unverified.

## The precedent

Apple has done this before, and the earlier cases show what a typical programme looks like. In 2018 it opened a display module replacement programme for the iPhone X after some units developed touchscreens that did not respond or reacted without being touched. In 2020 it did the same for a limited share of iPhone 11 handsets, defined by a manufacturing window running from November 2019 to May 2020. In both cases Apple defined eligibility by model and, in the iPhone 11 case, by build date, and owners could check their serial number on an Apple support page.

Those programmes were narrow and technical. Neither became a large financial event for the company. That is a reasonable baseline for this one, but it is only a baseline: the present programme may be larger or smaller, and nothing published so far says which.

## Why scale decides the story

Two numbers would turn this from a footnote into a story: how many handsets are covered, and how old they are. A programme limited to a few months of production is a modest repair bill. One spanning a full model year, or several, implies a design or supplier problem and a larger cost, along with a harder question about how the fault got past testing.

There is also a consumer-trust angle. Phones are a premium product sold partly on durability, and a replacement programme is, in effect, an admission that some units did not meet that standard. The way Apple handles it, including how clearly it communicates and how easy it makes the claim, tends to matter more to owners than the fault itself.

## What to watch

The first thing to look for is Apple's own support notice, which would name the models, the eligibility window and the process for claiming. The second is whether the programme is time-limited. The 2018 iPhone X scheme ran for three years from the phone's first retail sale, so the length of the window would hint at how seriously Apple rates the fault. Until the notice appears, the programme remains a brief item with the details still to come.

glp1-needles-recycling-warning.headline: Weight-loss jab boom brings needle-disposal warning for recyclers
glp1-needles-recycling-warning.body_md:
Used needles from weight-loss injections are turning up in household recycling, and the people who sort that material are the ones most likely to find them. Waste-industry and pharmacy-trade reports describe the problem. A BBC UK report, which this piece could not read directly, is understood to have raised it too.

The drugs are GLP-1 medicines such as Wegovy, Ozempic and Mounjaro. They are injected weekly with a pen device carrying a fine needle. Whatever the number of UK users, each one generates a steady supply of sharps. Those sharps are meant to go into a dedicated bin. Some are going into the blue bin, or the general bin, instead.

## What the waste sector is reporting

The trade publication *letsrecycle* has run headlines on the issue, including one describing weight-loss jabs as a "growing challenge for waste sector". Sherbourne Recycling in Coventry is reported to have seen more sharps in its collections, including weight-loss pens. It runs a facility that handles roughly 175,000 tonnes of mixed household waste a year. The operator warns that wrongly discarded sharps put crews and sorters at risk of needle-stick injury. These figures come from search summaries of the reports, not from the original articles, and should be checked before reuse.

No reliable national count of incidents has been found. Neither has a verified figure for how many pens enter recycling. One widely repeated trade estimate says up to 6 million GLP-1 pens a year could end up in landfill. That is an estimate of pens discarded, not of needle-stick injuries. It also concerns landfill, not recycling streams, so it does not measure this particular problem.

Sorting lines are where the risk concentrates. Material arrives mixed and is often handled by hand or fed through machinery that crews must clear. A needle hidden in a bag of plastic is hard to see. Needle-stick injuries carry a small but real risk of blood-borne infection. Even where no infection follows, injured workers typically face anxious follow-up testing.

## What users are supposed to do

NHS-linked prescribing guidance from several integrated care boards says anyone injecting insulin or a GLP-1 medicine should have a sharps bin. It adds that collection of full bins is arranged through the local authority. Arrangements vary by area, so a council's own web page is the authority for any given household.

Pharmacy guidance is less uniform on the pen body. For Mounjaro, one pharmacy guide advises putting the whole pen in the sharps bin with the needle still attached. Guides for Saxenda suggest returning empty pens to a pharmacy or following council advice. Novo Nordisk is reported to have run a take-back scheme for its plastic pens at Boots stores, with needles removed first and binned. The current status of that scheme is unconfirmed. These are secondary sources, not NHS pages.

The consistent point is that pens and needles do not belong in household recycling. Pharmacy-trade guidance also says that putting sharps in household waste breaches the Environmental Protection Act 1990. That legal claim comes from trade press and has not been checked against the statute.

## Who pays

The likely effect is to push a clinical disposal task onto services designed for kitchen packaging. Councils may face more injuries, more screening of loads and more public-information work. Some trade voices have called for a national disposal scheme, though a specific proposal has not been verified here.

The pattern has an American precedent. New York's sanitation department is reported to be seeking to raise the fine for improperly discarded needles from $100 to $250 after workers were stuck. Recycling plant workers in Washington state have reported similar injuries, mostly from insulin needles. Neither case shows what is happening in Britain. They do show that the same pressure appears wherever injectable prescribing grows.

## What is missing

The piece cannot yet say how many UK councils have recorded GLP-1-related sharps, how many workers have been hurt, or how many people use the drugs. An on-record statement from a council or a waste-worker body is still needed. So is the current official guidance from the NHS or the relevant regulator. Any of those would turn a plausible trend into a measured one. For now, the practical advice is plain: the needle goes in a sharps bin, and the bin goes back through the route the local council or pharmacy specifies.

leeds-muharemovic-estevao.headline: Leeds close in on Muharemovic as Chelsea's Estevao becomes the forgotten man
leeds-muharemovic-estevao.body_md:
Two Premier League squad stories are doing the rounds on the BBC Sport football pages: Leeds United are reported to be close to signing a player named Muharemovic, and Chelsea's Estevao is being described as the club's "forgotten man". Neither story involves a confirmed deal, a fee or a club statement. This is rumour territory, and it is labelled that way here.

## Leeds and Muharemovic

The BBC Sport headline says Leeds are "close" to a deal for Muharemovic. That is all the available reporting establishes. The first name, the selling club, the fee and the contract length are not in the material seen for this piece, and none of them can responsibly be filled in from memory.

"Close" is a flexible word in transfer coverage. It can mean a medical is booked, or it can mean two clubs have exchanged a polite email. Until Leeds announce something, or a fee and agreed terms are reported, the accurate position is that interest is advanced and a signing is possible, not done.

It is also worth noting what has not appeared: no quotes from Leeds, from the player or from his representatives. A signing that is truly imminent usually produces at least a flurry of "here we go" confirmations from the usual reliable sources. Their absence from this account does not mean the deal is off, but it does mean the story rests on a single headline.

## Estevao, out of view

The Chelsea item is different in kind. It is less a transfer story than a status story. Estevao, the club's young winger, is described as the "forgotten man", with questions over what his role at Stamford Bridge actually is.

That phrase is the BBC's framing, and it carries its own caveat. "Forgotten" is a judgement about playing time and prominence, not a statement from Chelsea about his future. No manager's comment, minutes tally or club line has been put forward here to back it up, so the reasons behind it remain open. Selection, form, fitness and squad depth can all push a young attacker down the pecking order, and a headline cannot tell them apart.

What can fairly be said is that a young winger being left out of the picture is a story squads of Chelsea's size produce every season. It becomes a larger one only if it leads somewhere: a loan, a change of role, or an open statement from the manager about where he fits.

## What would change the picture

For Leeds, the trigger is simple: an official announcement, or credible reporting of an agreed fee and personal terms. Either would turn a modest squad story into a signing worth a proper write-up, including what the player offers and where he would slot in.

For Chelsea, the useful development would be a substantive report on Estevao himself. That means the manager explaining his selection choices, or word of a loan or other move. Until then, the label "forgotten man" describes a mood more than a fact.

One caution applies to both stories. Supporters of either club will be tempted to read a great deal into two headlines. The evidence so far supports very little: one deal that may be near, and one player whose standing is being questioned.

red-roses-six-changes.headline: Red Roses make six changes, with Kildunne on the bench again
red-roses-six-changes.body_md:
England's Red Roses have made six changes to the side named for their next fixture. Ellie Kildunne, the full-back who has been central to the team's attack for several seasons, is on the bench again.

That is the extent of what could be confirmed. The BBC Sport headline gives the numbers, but this report could not verify the opponent, the date, the venue, the full list of changes or the reasons behind them. A search for the team sheet turned up earlier Red Roses selections but nothing matching this one. The details below are therefore limited to what the headline supports.

## What the word 'again' implies

The headline says Kildunne is on the bench *again*, which means she was also among the replacements last time out. One bench place can be rotation. Two in a row looks more like a pattern, and a pattern invites a question: is it a tactical call, a fitness management plan, or a sign that someone else has taken the shirt?

The team sheet alone cannot settle that. Selection notes from the head coach, John Mitchell, usually say whether a player is being managed or simply left out of the starting XV. Until that explanation is on the record, any reading of the bench place is guesswork.

## Six changes in context

Six is a middling number by Red Roses standards. In recent seasons England have swung between heavy rotation, with a dozen or more changes in games where the result was not in doubt, and tightly held line-ups in knockout matches. Six sits between the two, and a change count says little without the fixture's stakes attached.

The useful questions are where the changes fall. A reshuffled back three would mean something different from fresh faces in the front row. The same goes for whether the changes come from injury or are chosen. None of that can be answered from the headline.

## What to watch

The full team sheet and Mitchell's explanation are the immediate tests. The first will show who is in the starting XV and who has taken Kildunne's usual place. The second should say whether her bench role is a rest, a fitness precaution or a straight selection decision. Her minutes in the match itself will tell the rest: an early introduction would suggest a plan, while a late one would suggest she has slipped down the order. This piece will be updated once the details are confirmed.

russell-brand-trial-testimony.headline: Russell Brand tells trial it was wrong to use fame to 'facilitate' sex
russell-brand-trial-testimony.body_md:
Russell Brand, the comedian and former broadcaster, has told the jury at his criminal trial that it was wrong to use his fame to "facilitate" sex, according to the Guardian's report of his evidence. He denies every charge against him.

The remark is a notable one in a courtroom. Defendants rarely volunteer moral concessions while contesting allegations of rape and sexual assault. The line between conduct a witness regards as regrettable and conduct the law treats as criminal is the one a jury will be asked to draw.

This article rests on the Guardian's account of the testimony. The exact wording, and the question that prompted it, have not been checked against a court transcript. The headline's phrasing is the newspaper's, not a verified quotation.

## The case

Brand was charged in April 2025 with rape and sexual assault offences involving four women. The alleged offences date from roughly 1999 to 2005, the years when he was building a career across stand-up, radio and television. He has consistently denied the allegations, and he is presumed innocent.

The trial was listed at Southwark Crown Court for 2026, with a start expected in June. Whether proceedings are at the stage of his own evidence, as the Guardian's report implies, is for the court record to establish. Nothing here should be read as a finding on any count.

## Fame and consent

What gives the testimony its wider interest is the subject it touches: whether celebrity, as a form of power, shapes encounters that are later disputed. That question has run through the entertainment industry's reckoning of recent years, in courts, in newsroom investigations and in workplace policy.

A defendant describing fame as something he used, and saying that was wrong, does not settle that debate. In law, conduct that is morally questionable is not the same as an offence. The jury will be directed on that distinction, and on the standard of proof, when the evidence closes. Admissions of poor behaviour can be used by either side: a prosecution may argue they show a pattern, while a defence may argue they show candour.

The case changes no law and moves no market. Its reach is to readers of culture and legal news, and to a long-running argument about influence in show business.

## What to watch

The next markers are the remainder of the cross-examination, the closing speeches and the judge's summing-up. The jury's verdicts on each count, delivered separately, will decide the matter. Reporting restrictions and the court's own timetable govern what can be published until then.
russell-brand-trial-testimony.in_one_sentence: Russell Brand, who denies all charges, reportedly told his trial it was wrong to use fame to 'facilitate' sex, though the wording awaits checking against the court record.

rosebank-labour-backbench-rift.headline: Labour MPs urge No 10 not to overrule the energy secretary on Rosebank
rosebank-labour-backbench-rift.body_md:
Labour backbenchers are lobbying Downing Street not to overrule the energy secretary if she refuses permission for Rosebank, the large undeveloped oil field west of Shetland. The dispute is partly about one field. It is also a test of who holds the final say on North Sea licensing, and of how far the government will bend its climate commitments under pressure from the Treasury.

## Who is deciding

The energy secretary is Miatta Fahnbulleh, not Ed Miliband, who held the post when the consent problem first arose. According to sources cited by the Guardian on 21 October, she is "minded" to refuse environmental permission for Rosebank. No decision has been announced. Her aides say she is the sole decision-maker.

The decision is back with ministers because the Court of Session quashed Rosebank's original consent in January 2025. The court found that the developers had not assessed scope 3 emissions, meaning those released when the oil is burned. A fresh assessment has been under way since.

The government approved the smaller Jackdaw gasfield last week. Prime Minister Andy Burnham described it as "a bridge to the future". Fahnbulleh has argued that Jackdaw is a gasfield serving the domestic market, while Rosebank is mainly an export oilfield, so the same reasoning does not carry over.

## The backbench case

The Guardian reports that Labour MPs have been pressing both the prime minister and the chancellor to leave her ruling alone. Burnham says the decision is Fahnbulleh's. But his Commons remarks on Jackdaw led some ministers to read his promise of a "pragmatic" approach to oil and gas as a sign he would support Rosebank. Chancellor John Healey is reportedly in favour of the scheme, according to sources close to him.

Catherine Fookes, a Labour member of the energy select committee, said: "Approving Rosebank will blow a hole in our green credentials." Clive Lewis questioned whether the Treasury's expected tax receipts can be trusted, since they rest on operator estimates. One MP warned of a major rebellion if Healey pushed the project through.

MPs were willing to accept Jackdaw because it was framed around domestic gas supply. Their objection is that Rosebank is a different case.

## The Treasury's numbers

The Treasury expects about £500m in tax revenue from Rosebank by the end of this parliament, a figure that has appeared in Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts since 2019. The OBR says oil and gas output would fall by roughly 14% a year without new fields.

The campaign group Uplift argues the tax take may be limited, and could be eroded by tax allowances and decommissioning costs. Areeba Hamid of Greenpeace UK says future revenues would leave public services exposed to oil prices, and taxpayers liable for decommissioning bills.

Some in government argue she can approve the field without breaching carbon commitments. Their reasoning is that most of the oil would be exported, and emissions from burning it abroad do not count against UK targets. That is the very question the court ruling put at the centre of the case, and critics are likely to say it sidesteps the scope 3 finding.

Aberdeen South MP Douglas Lumsden, who backs the field, has written to the energy secretary calling a refusal "cruel, unnecessary and uneconomic". Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra has also urged approval.

## What to watch

The immediate question is whether Fahnbulleh issues a ruling, and whether Downing Street or the Treasury intervenes if she refuses. Any ruling would set a precedent for other North Sea applications that depend on the same end-use emissions assessment. An overruling would also test the line that the decision belongs to the energy secretary alone. Much of the reporting rests on private briefings, so the reported leanings may change before a formal announcement.

neonatal-parent-meals-policy.headline: Mother of critically ill baby denied hospital food because she wasn't breastfeeding
neonatal-parent-meals-policy.body_md:
A mother whose newborn daughter was critically ill in a Welsh hospital says she was refused a meal because she was not breastfeeding. She has called the rule outdated. The health board says its policy is to feed breastfeeding mothers, and that ward teams can give other parents basic food case by case.

The account comes from BBC Wales, published on 29 October. It has not been independently verified, and the health board's written policy has not been published. What follows rests on the BBC report and the board's statement to it.

## What happened

Sophie Price, 22, from Newport, gave birth at Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran, Torfaen. About five days later her daughter, Florence, was on a paediatric ward. Ms Price says she was told she was no longer a patient and would not be given meals, because she was not breastfeeding. She had by then gone about 28 hours without eating.

The report describes a difficult recovery. She was bleeding and in significant pain, had had her hips put back in place after dislocating them during the birth, and had fluid build-up (oedema) in her feet that made walking hard.

Florence was diagnosed with bronchiolitis, rhinovirus and a blood infection. Her lungs could not work unaided, and she was put on a machine that pushed air into them through a mask. Her parents were told she might need to be put into an induced coma at any point. The family spent about three weeks in hospital. Ms Price left for 24 hours, then returned when Florence stopped breathing properly.

Relatives took turns to bring food around their working hours, and the family says it spent more than £1,000 on canteen meals and takeaways. Her husband, Ryli, had paternity leave that was running out during the stay.

## The rule

According to the BBC's account of the health board's position, the distinction turns on who counts as the patient. On a maternity ward, mother and baby both do, so meals are provided whether or not the mother breastfeeds. On a paediatric ward only the child is the patient. The board says its policy is to provide meals to breastfeeding mothers there, because this supports the baby's feeding.

That rationale has a logic to it, but it leaves a group uncovered. A mother who is formula feeding, or whose baby is too ill to feed at all, falls outside it, though she may be as tied to the bedside as anyone. Ms Price calls the policy "outdated" and says it discriminates against mothers who formula-feed. She wants hospitals to provide meals to all mothers regardless of how they feed.

Formula was a second point of dispute. The board says it is "provided as needed". Ms Price says staff told her she would have to bring her own. After her mother contacted the hospital, it continued to supply formula for Florence.

## The health board's response

Aneurin Bevan University Health Board said it was "sorry to hear about Sophie's experience" and is committed to supporting families. It said ward teams can provide basic food and refreshments where parents cannot reach the canteen, have limited support or cannot leave the bedside. It also pointed to a ward voucher scheme for discounted meals, said financial hardship can be raised with ward staff, and said requests are considered case by case.

The gap between the stated policy and Ms Price's experience is the crux. If the discretion exists, it was not offered here, or not offered clearly. A rule that relies on parents knowing to ask, while they are frightened and exhausted, will reach some families and miss others.

## What remains unclear

The BBC report names one health board. The wording of the policy, how often discretion is used and whether other trusts apply similar rules are not established. Earlier complaints of a similar kind have surfaced in patient-feedback posts and local reports in Wales and Scotland, but those are anecdotal and cannot be assumed to reflect current practice.

The next test is whether Aneurin Bevan publishes its catering criteria or revises them, and whether other boards are asked to say how they treat non-breastfeeding parents on children's and neonatal wards.

japan-haunted-homes-discounts.headline: Japan's haunted homes attract bargain-hunting buyers
japan-haunted-homes-discounts.body_md:
In Japan, a death in a house can cut its price. Buyers have noticed, and a growing number are treating the stigma as a bargain.

The trade is in what the market calls *jiko bukken*, or "incident properties": homes and flats where someone has died by murder, suicide or an unattended death, often a lonely one. Disclosure law generally obliges agents to say so. That obligation, together with a reluctance to live in a place with a dark history, pushes prices below those of comparable homes.

## How big is the discount?

There is no official national statistic, and the figures that circulate are indicative rather than systematic. A property expert quoted by Reuters in 2025 described one house as priced about 20% below the market because of its history. Village House, a rental agency, puts suicide-related discounts at 10% to 30%, depending on whether the death was inside a unit or in a common area. A July 2026 Business Today report cites roughly 30% in big cities and up to 50% or more in smaller towns. Brokers have said the worst cases, such as murder sites, can fall much further or fail to sell at all.

The spread is wide, which is itself informative. The discount appears to depend on how the person died, where the property is and how many alternatives buyers have.

## Why now

The backdrop is demographic. Japan's population has fallen since its 2008 peak, and the 2023 housing survey counted roughly 9 million vacant homes, about 13.8% of the national stock. When supply of empty houses is that abundant, sellers have less room to hold out for a clean-slate price, and a stigma that once made a property unsellable becomes something to negotiate over.

The Economist, as quoted on an online forum, notes that a death need not be disclosed after three years, so a discounted property can later be resold at full price. Several firms now do business around the stigma: specialists who spend nights in a home to show it holds no lingering spirits, and others who offer ceremonies for lost souls. That would turn the taboo into a service line as well as a price signal.

## What to watch

The limits are plain. This is a niche corner of a market where plenty of vacant homes are simply unwanted, haunted or not, and some akiya are on offer for next to nothing regardless of their history. The test of the "stigma trade" is whether buyers who pay 20% to 30% less can resell without the discount, as the three-year rule implies. Without systematic transaction data, which does not yet exist, the evidence is anecdotal. The next housing survey, and any move by regulators to collect figures on incident properties, would show whether this is a durable pricing category or a curiosity.

fleetwood-league-cup-quarter-final.headline: Fleetwood to face Everton or Newcastle in the League Cup quarter-final
fleetwood-league-cup-quarter-final.body_md:
Fleetwood Town, a League Two club, have reached the League Cup quarter-finals for the first time in their history. They did it by knocking out the reigning Premier League champions, Arsenal. The draw has now been made, and the opponent is still open. Fleetwood will play the winner of Everton against Newcastle United, which is the last fourth-round tie and is due to be played at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Thursday.

The triage note described Fleetwood as a League One side. That is wrong: the club is in League Two, which makes the draw a bigger story than a routine lower-league cup tie.

## The upset that made the draw

Arsenal went to Highbury Stadium on Tuesday night and left without winning. Aaron Loupalo-Bi put Fleetwood ahead in the 21st minute. Viktor Gyökeres levelled early in the second half. The tie then went to penalties, and Fleetwood won the shootout 5-3, scoring all five of their kicks. Conor Haughey took the decisive one.

The result is the kind League Cup nights are remembered for. A fourth-tier side took down the champions, and the neutral gets a shock to talk about. Arsenal, for their part, were left to reflect on a bad night. Mikel Arteta described the exit as a "very sad day" in a headline quoted by one outlet, though the full remarks were not available to check.

## The draw

The quarter-final ties, as drawn, are:

- Fleetwood Town v Everton or Newcastle United
- Manchester City v Bradford City
- Crystal Palace v Sunderland
- Liverpool v Bournemouth

Fleetwood have been drawn at home, so the winner of the Merseyside-or-Tyneside tie will travel to Highbury Stadium. That is a neat reward for a club that has just beaten Arsenal there. Bradford City, another lower-league side, will visit Manchester City.

The either/or wording on Fleetwood's tie is not stale information. The draw was made before the last fourth-round game had been played, so one pairing was left open by design.

## What comes next

Everton and Newcastle settle the matter on Thursday. The quarter-finals are due in the week commencing 14 December, with some reports suggesting 15 to 17 December. The exact date and kick-off times have not been confirmed.

Whoever comes through will arrive at a ground that has just seen the champions beaten. Fleetwood will have six weeks or so to prepare and to enjoy it.

george-michael-auction-row.headline: Family row over George Michael items, including the Faith guitar, at auction
george-michael-auction-row.body_md:
A row inside George Michael's family has surfaced on the day a collection of his memorabilia, headed by the guitar from the video for "Faith", goes under the hammer. BBC News reports a dispute over the sale. At the time of writing, the public record does not say who is objecting, on what grounds, or whether the auction will go ahead as scheduled.

## The sale

The items are being offered by Sworders, the Essex auction house, in a sale titled *Faith & Fame: A Personal George Michael Collection*, scheduled for 29 October 2026. The centrepiece is a 1940s Gretsch Synchromatic 160, the guitar the singer carried in the 1987 video. The house has put its estimate at £60,000 to £120,000.

The lots did not come from the singer's estate. According to coverage of the sale, the archive was assembled by Siobhan Bailey, Michael's personal assistant for some two decades, who died in 2014. It is her widower who is selling. The guitar's story is part of the appeal: Guitar World's account of the instrument says it spent years in a garage with other memorabilia after the Faith tour.

## What is and isn't known

The BBC's report is the only one found that describes a family dispute, and its details could not be independently confirmed. Nothing in the sale material reviewed names a claimant or a legal challenge.

Sworders' own line on the guitar has been that its provenance is secure. Its chairman, Guy Schooling, was quoted in pre-sale coverage as saying the family agreed this was the original video guitar, so its authenticity "won't ever be contested". That concerns authenticity, not ownership or the right to sell. A disagreement about who is entitled to dispose of the objects, or about how they left Michael's possession, would be a separate matter, and the available material does not address it.

## What to watch

The practical questions are narrow. Auction houses facing a claim to title typically withdraw a lot or hold the proceeds until the matter is resolved; a sale that proceeds with the guitar intact would suggest Sworders regards the challenge as weak or aimed elsewhere. Any statement from the auctioneer, the Bailey family or Michael's relatives on the day would settle which it is. The hammer price will also say something: the guitar's estimate is £60,000 to £120,000, and a figure well below that would suggest buyers were wary of a contested lot.

For now, the sale is listed for today, and the dispute is a headline without a case file behind it.

montenegro-embassy-planning-challenge.headline: Neighbour of new Montenegro embassy in London sues council over mental-health impact
montenegro-embassy-planning-challenge.body_md:
A woman who lives next door to Montenegro's new embassy in Pimlico, central London, is taking Westminster City Council to the High Court. She argues it failed to weigh what the embassy's arrival would do to her mental health when it dealt with the building's planning.

Diana Simpson, 35, a Stanford graduate, lives on Cambridge Street with her parents. Her father is a former US diplomat who has lived on the street for more than 30 years. She has applied for judicial review and potential damages, according to the Guardian's report, which was syndicated by AOL. Mr Justice Mould is hearing the case.

## A family home, then an embassy

The embassy has moved into a five-bedroom family home on the street. The change of use, and the flagpole that came with it, were in place before planning permission was sought. Residents objected to the flag and a plaque. The Montenegrin chargé d'affaires responded by hosting drinks for neighbours, which, by the account of the case, did not settle every concern.

Simpson receives disability benefits for clinical anxiety, long Covid and a functional neurological disorder. She says her sleep is regularly disrupted and that she sometimes moves to a different room. She describes waking with a fear of intruders from the embassy, which she calls "mostly irrational". She has considered whether she can stay in the house, which she had expected to be a long-term home.

## The legal grounds

Her claim rests on several points. She says the council breached human rights and equality law. She also says it acted irrationally and ran a flawed consultation, and that it approached objections with a closed mind once the Foreign Office had given its permission.

Westminster denies the allegations. It says there is "no plausible interference" with her home or her private and family life, and it is seeking summary judgment, which would end the case without a full hearing. A council spokesperson said councils must decide in line with planning policy and declined further comment at this stage.

The claim tests an unusual question for planning law: how far a decision-maker must consider an individual neighbour's health, as opposed to the usual planning concerns of noise, traffic and visual impact. The summary-judgment application suggests the council thinks the answer is "not here".

## Not the first embassy row

London's embassies often sit in converted houses, and neighbours do not always welcome them. Turkmenistan's embassy in an adapted family home on Victoria Road, Kensington, drew complaints about consultation and courtesy. North Korea has run an embassy for about two decades in a seven-bedroom 1920s house in Ealing, where neighbours report no problems.

I could not see the court filings or the planning file. The date of any hearing on the summary-judgment application is not given in the reporting. If the court grants that application, the claim ends early. If it refuses, the council will have to defend its handling of the application in full.

german-wildlife-park-wolf-attack.headline: Girl seriously hurt in wolf attack at German wildlife park
german-wildlife-park-wolf-attack.body_md:
An eight-year-old girl was seriously injured by a wolf on Wednesday at a private wildlife park south of Berlin. She was flown to hospital by rescue helicopter. The park is shut while the district reviews how it operates.

The attack happened on 28 October at the Wildpark Johannismühle, near Baruth/Mark in Brandenburg, about 45 km from the capital. The girl was one of three taking part in a booked children's animal-keeper day, held before the park opened to the public. With a female keeper, they were in the polar wolf enclosure while the animals were being given water, according to the Teltow-Fläming district. At least one wolf attacked the girl, and police later confirmed it was a wolf.

The keeper reportedly stepped in quickly and stopped the animals reaching the other two girls. Those present, other than the injured child, were reported physically unharmed. Emergency counsellors looked after four people, three of them children.

## What the review is asking

The central question is how three children came to be inside a predator enclosure at all. Police are investigating that, and whether negligence played a part. The district says it will examine the park's safety measures and operating procedures. The park stays closed until the responsible authority approves reopening, and the veterinary office will carry out an animal-welfare inspection.

The paper trail so far is clean. The county's last on-site inspection, on 23 July 2025, found no safety-relevant defects in fences or enclosures. The park says its security fences are checked every morning before opening, and its operating permit requires daily checks of predator and bison enclosures for weak points. That points away from a broken fence as the cause. The focus is on the arrangement itself: a guided programme that put children in with the animals.

No expert assessment of the wolves' health or behaviour exists yet. The girl's condition has not been detailed publicly, and the park has said only that it regrets the incident, is cooperating fully and is supporting the family. It has declined further comment while proceedings continue.

## A local story, for now

The park keeps grey and polar wolves, along with deer, roe deer, a brown bear and a lynx. Wolf bites on people are rare in Germany. A boy of eight was bitten on the chest at the Filmtierpark Eschede in Lower Saxony in 2023, after a wolf sniffed his hand and then snapped. That episode, like this one, involved a captive animal and a close encounter arranged for visitors.

On current evidence this remains a single-site incident. It would become a wider story only if the review finds that supervised, hands-on sessions with predators are run on thin rules elsewhere, or that the permit conditions leave gaps. Whether any of that applies is not established.

What to watch: the police finding on how the children entered the enclosure, the district's decision on reopening, and whether the veterinary inspection leads to changes in how parks offer keeper-style experiences near wolves.

floor.headline: Mean-reverter's gains rode on one trade, and maybe a headline
floor.body_md:
A quiet day with one loud trade. The mean-reverter closed four positions in the uk-eu shadow book, and most of the gain came from MLL.DE, which reached its take-profit and did the heavy lifting alone. EDBL also hit its target and posted the larger percentage move, though the bot's own notes suggest a headline may have pushed it as much as the oversold reading did.

The losers were the more instructive pair. EVSBY and ATSI.MC both ran to their scheduled exits with prices barely moved. The snap-back never came, and the small losses were most likely spreads and fees. A washed-out chart is not a timer. Tomorrow's question is whether the strategy can tell a flush that reverts from one that just sits there. Today it showed it can cash in on the first kind.

floor.headline: Five losses, no winners, and two trades that never moved
floor.body_md: The shadow book had a flat, unforgiving day. All five ml-challenger trades closed red, and none closed with the move the model had called for. NA and BIVI exited exactly where they entered, so their predicted rallies never arrived. The thesis went untested rather than refuted. Their small losses look like friction (spreads, fees, currency conversion) rather than price action, and a low-priced name can carry stale quotes. FUUFF took the heaviest loss of the group, yet the ledger's notes say nothing about it, and that gap deserves closing before anyone reads much into it. Nothing here shows a model that was right but early, or wrong and late. Tomorrow's test is simple: do the flat exits repeat? If they do, check the pricing feed and exit logic before blaming the signal.
